tldr: The authors introduce DexSuite, an open-source, Genesis-based simulation framework and a 4,700-episode dataset designed to compare multi-fingered hands and parallel-jaw grippers under identical tasks and evaluation metrics. The experiments demonstrate that higher degrees of freedom in dexterous hands do not inherently hurt imitation learning performance. However, multi-stage tasks with sequential contacts and precise tool use remain major open challenges.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of DexSuite. Built on top of the Genesis simulator, it enables modular, dynamic assembly of robotic arms and end-effectors (grippers and dexterous hands). Decoupling task logic and success criteria from specific robot embodiments enables fair comparisons in identical environments.
overview:
Human living spaces are built for dexterous human hands. Yet, most robot manipulation research has historically relied on two-finger parallel-jaw grippers because they are easier to model and collect data for. Dexterous hands have high degrees of freedom, complex intermittent contacts, and pronounced Sim-to-Real gaps. As a result, task definitions and data collection workflows have remained fragmented across different research groups.

To tackle this, the authors developed DexSuite, an all-in-one simulation framework that covers the full pipeline of learning, evaluation, and data collection for dexterous manipulation. Built on Genesis—a lightweight and fast physics simulator—DexSuite lets users dynamically combine 10 arms and 12 end-effectors into more than 100 single-arm robots and thousands of bimanual configurations.

The paper also defines a benchmark of 16 task-embodiment pairs. This includes 5 shared tasks that fairly evaluate the performance gap between grippers and multi-fingered hands, alongside 6 challenging tasks that demand true multi-fingered dexterity. The authors release a dataset of 4,700 successful trajectories gathered via human teleoperation, scripted policies, and learned rollouts, and evaluate popular imitation learning algorithms such as Diffusion Policy and ACT across the suite.

The findings show that increasing degrees of freedom does not necessarily make learning harder. However, tasks with sequential contacts across multiple objects, or those requiring fingertip-level precision like drilling to a target or spraying a can, lead to near-zero success rates with state-of-the-art imitation learning, highlighting substantial remaining bottlenecks.
contributions: Released DexSuite as an open-source, unified framework built on the Genesis simulator, supporting 30 diverse tasks and modular assembly of 10 arms and 12 end-effectors.
Established a 16-pair benchmark protocol featuring a cross-embodiment evaluation track with shared success criteria and a dedicated multi-fingered dexterity track.
Provided a multimodal dataset of 4,700 successful episodes collected from human teleoperation, scripted experts, and learned policy rollouts.

Systematically evaluated leading imitation learning algorithms (BC variants, Diffusion Policy, ACT) to reveal how hand degrees of freedom, task horizons, and sequential contacts affect policy success rates.

sections.heading: Why do we need a simulation framework centered on dexterous hands?
sections.summary: Multi-fingered hands are essential for robots operating in human spaces, yet research has long prioritized two-finger grippers. Because dexterous hands are hard to control and existing environments are deeply fragmented, DexSuite offers an integrated platform to fairly compare hands and grippers on the exact same tasks.
sections.details:
Human tools and environments were designed around the dexterity of human hands. While parallel-jaw grippers have achieved great success in basic pick-and-place tasks, they face fundamental limits in in-hand reorientation, multi-point contact stabilization, and compliant tool use.

If robots are to adapt to human environments rather than forcing environments to adapt to robots, dexterous hands must become first-class benchmark targets. Simulators are crucial because hardware experiments break easily and do not scale well. Yet, most popular benchmarks and large-scale datasets continue to prioritize parallel-jaw grippers.

The reason is obvious. Multi-fingered hands have high actuator degrees of freedom (DoF), involve intermittent object contacts, are sensitive to physics modeling errors, and are far harder to teleoperate, train, and evaluate. Consequently, prior work often stayed confined to isolated tasks tailored to a single specific hand model. It was nearly impossible to swap a gripper for a hand on the exact same task for a fair comparison.

To address this gap, DexSuite unifies task definitions and provides integrated teleoperation demonstrations. The authors use it to investigate three core questions: (1) Can policies for multi-fingered hands match gripper success rates on identical tasks? (2) How much do longer horizons and sequential contacts degrade hand performance? (3) Which tasks requiring fine fingertip control remain out of reach for current imitation learning?

sections.heading: The fragmentation bottleneck in existing simulators and dexterous benchmarks
sections.summary: Existing robotic learning environments separate arm-gripper setups from multi-fingered hands, while bimanual manipulation remains scattered across different tools. In addition, large-scale datasets focus heavily on gripper arm motions, leaving a gap where hands and grippers can rarely be compared head-to-head.
sections.details:
Examining previous work across simulators, benchmarks, and datasets clarifies the primary goals of DexSuite.

### II-A Manipulation simulators
Platforms like Isaac Lab and ManiSkill3 enable massive GPU-parallel training, while robosuite and RLBench provide standardized APIs and rich task sets. Frameworks like RoboCasa and OmniGibson recreate photorealistic home environments. However, these environments generally decouple arm-gripper tasks from dexterous hand tasks, and bimanual setups are fragmented across different frameworks. Almost no existing interface lets researchers simply swap end-effectors within the same scene and conditions to evaluate performance shifts.

### II-B Dexterous manipulation benchmarks
Notable multi-fingered benchmarks include DexArt for articulated objects, DexMV for human-to-robot video retargeting, and Dactyl or DAPG for reinforcement learning on in-hand reorientation. Yet, these efforts were almost exclusively tied to a single hand model. Even Bi-DexHands, which targets bimanual dexterity, uses floating Shadow Hands decoupled from realistic arm setups.

### II-C Datasets for imitation and offline learning
Recent large-scale datasets like DROID and Open X-Embodiment have significantly advanced generalist policy learning. However, they almost exclusively feature parallel-jaw grippers and emphasize arm trajectory learning. Existing multi-fingered hand datasets are limited to narrow tasks, static grasps, or short horizons. Trajectory data covering long-horizon tasks under a unified observation and action space has been severely lacking.

DexSuite closes these gaps by uniting rigid, articulated, and deformable physics, tactile simulation, bimanual support, and dynamic runtime assembly of arms and hands into a single stack.

sections.heading: A modular simulation design that never breaks when swapping end-effectors
sections.summary: DexSuite builds on the Genesis simulator, fully decoupling task definitions from robot embodiments. It offers dynamic arm-hand assembly, workspace-aware object placement, realistic tactile simulation, and diverse teleoperation interfaces under a standard Gymnasium API.
sections.details:
DexSuite uses Genesis—a lightweight, Python-native simulator—as its physics, rendering, and parallel computation engine, building a reproducible experimentation layer for robot learning on top of it.

### III-A Environments
The suite provides 30 diverse tasks across two domains based on control requirements:
- Rigid-body objects (23 tasks): Reach, Lift, Push, Pick & Place, Stack, reorientation, and more. These demand accurate grasping and stable contact.
- Articulated objects (7 tasks): Folding glasses, opening jar lids, pushing down a toaster lever, closing windows, and similar tasks. Policies must understand internal kinematic constraints and exert force along joint limits.
In addition, models incorporate the YCB dataset with adjusted mass and center-of-mass properties, as well as novel objects and diverse friction and visual textures.

### III-B Embodiment Abstraction
Traditional frameworks often hardcode task logic and initial object layouts to a specific robot kinematic tree. DexSuite fundamentally abstracts this relationship:
- Dynamic Robot Assembly: With 10 arms and 12 end-effectors (including models from MuJoCo Menagerie), users can assemble over 100 single-arm robots and thousands of bimanual pairs at runtime. Arms are controlled via inverse kinematics (IK) and hands via joint position commands under a unified interface. The Tool Center Point (TCP) used for reward computation and success checks is standardized across end-effectors, defined at the fingertip midpoint for grippers and at a central grasp frame for multi-fingered hands.
- Workspace-Aware Sampling: Different robots have different reach envelopes. DexSuite assigns an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of reachable space to each arm, automatically scaling initial object placement areas to match the robot's reachable range. This prevents kinematic failures when changing hands or arms.

### III-C Data Collection and Interfaces
DexSuite also prioritizes versatile data collection and extensibility:
- Teleoperation: Arm poses can be driven by SpaceMouse, HTC Vive, or Meta Quest controllers. Finger motions support MediaPipe, Leap Motion, Quest hand tracking, and Manus MetaGlove Pro data gloves.
- Tactile Sensing: DexSuite simulates the FlexiTac sensor, featuring a 12×32 grid of pressure-sensitive taxels spaced at 2 mm across an elastomeric surface. It can be mounted on any link with a planar contact surface, outputting normal and shear forces based on object indentation.
- Extensibility: All environments conform to the standard Gymnasium API, making them directly compatible with existing reinforcement learning and imitation learning pipelines.

captions.F2: Simulated output of the FlexiTac tactile sensor mounted on a two-finger gripper during the Move Pan task. Normal and shear forces acting on the grasping surface are visualized in real time as pressure distributions across the taxel grid.
captions.F4: Diverse teleoperation devices integrated into DexSuite. Combining VR hardware like Meta Quest and HTC Vive, Manus data gloves, Leap Motion, SpaceMouse, and gamepads enables intuitive, simultaneous control of robotic arms and fingers.

sections.heading: 16 benchmark tasks and 4,700 multimodal trajectories decoupling embodiment from dexterity
sections.summary: The benchmark features 16 task-embodiment pairs: Track 1 (5 shared tasks) directly compares grippers and hands, while Track 2 (6 tasks) probes multi-fingered dexterity. They are paired with 4,700 high-quality success episodes collected via human teleoperation, scripts, and learned policies.
sections.details:
DexSuite's benchmark is structured to isolate the impact of hand dexterity step by step.

### IV-A Benchmark Design
The benchmark groups 11 distinct tasks into two tracks, forming 16 task-embodiment pairs:
- Track 1: Cross-Embodiment Evaluation: 5 simpler tasks achievable by both parallel-jaw grippers and multi-fingered hands (16-DoF Allegro Hand)—Reach, Lift, Push, Pick & Place, and Stack. Using identical task definitions and success criteria, this track directly evaluates the effect of changing only the end-effector.
- Track 2: Multi-fingered Dexterous Capability: 6 complex tasks whose shapes preclude standard parallel-jaw grasping. Four tasks use the Allegro Hand: Move Pan, Rack Mug, Place Fruits into a bowl, and Drill to Point. Two highly intricate tasks—Toast Bread and Spray Graffiti—employ the 22-DoF Sharpa Wave Hand.

### IV-B The DexSuite Dataset
The authors release 4,700 successful episodes covering all 16 benchmark pairs across three tiers:
- Human teleoperation demonstrations (700 episodes): Collected using the Robotiq gripper, UMI gripper, and Allegro Hand.
- Scripted demonstrations (1,200 episodes): Precision trajectories captured using the UMI gripper and Sharpa Hand.
- Policy rollouts (2,800 episodes): Autonomous successful trajectories from trained policies.
Every trajectory records proprioception, object states, front camera views, and wrist camera views. A subset of the scripted data also includes fingertip tactile readings. Data is formatted in standard LeRobot and robomimic (HDF5) formats.

captions.F3: Overview of tasks in the DexSuite benchmark. The top row shows Track 1 (Reach, Lift, Push, Pick & Place, Stack), which compares grippers and multi-fingered hands. The bottom row shows Track 2 (Move Pan, Rack Mug, Place Fruits, Drill to Point, Toast Bread, Spray Graffiti), designed to evaluate specialized multi-fingered dexterity.

sections.heading: Exposing imitation learning limits: Sequential contacts challenge policies more than hand DoF
sections.summary: Evaluating popular imitation learning algorithms showed that moving to multi-fingered hands does not inherently hurt performance. However, success rates plummeted on tasks with sequential multi-object contacts, precise drill alignment, and spray can tool manipulation, exposing clear algorithmic limitations.
sections.details:
The authors evaluated five baseline algorithms from robomimic: Behavior Cloning variants (BC-Gaussian, BC-GMM, BC-Transformer), Diffusion Policy, and ACT.

### V-A Experiment Setup
Policies were trained on 50 human teleoperation demonstrations (or 200 scripted demonstrations for the two long-horizon tasks). BC variants used state observations, ACT used images with proprioception, and Diffusion Policy was tested on both state and image inputs.
Importantly, the authors adopted a rigorous evaluation protocol. Rather than simply reporting the highest single checkpoint observed during training, they re-evaluated the best checkpoint across 3 new random seeds (50 episodes each, 150 trials total). For ACT, this revealed a gap of roughly 7 percentage points between the peak validation score and the true re-evaluated mean, underscoring the danger of ranking methods based on single checkpoint spikes.

### V-B Results
Three key takeaways emerge from the empirical results:

### Embodiment gap
A higher-dimensional hand action space does not automatically degrade learning. In the Push task, the Allegro Hand outperformed grippers across all six policy-observation configurations. The palm and spread fingers formed a wider contact surface, stabilizing the push. Conversely, grippers held an advantage in 4 settings on the Lift task. On Pick & Place, outcomes split by method: BC-T performed better with the hand (76% vs 64%), while ACT favored the gripper (60% vs 66%). Thus, the embodiment gap depends strongly on how task geometry interacts with the algorithm.

### Horizon and sequential manipulation
A sharp drop in performance occurred when tasks required manipulating multiple objects in sequence. In the Stack task, the best state-based policy reached only 16% on the gripper and 9% on Allegro, while image-based models peaked at just 2%. In Place Fruits, ACT topped out at 27%.
Interestingly, in Move Pan—a task with a comparable horizon of 500 to 600 steps involving a single object—ACT achieved an 89% success rate. Stage failure breakdowns show that in Stack, 22% to 30% of failures happened during the first block placement, and 12% to 24% failed on the second block. This proves that breaking contact with one object to initiate contact with another is what severely trips up current imitation learning.

### Dexterous capability
Some dexterous-only tasks succeeded well: state-based Diffusion achieved 82% on Rack Mug, and ACT hit 89% on Move Pan. However, tool-use tasks revealed sharp limitations.
On Drill to Point, even when policies grasped the drill, 48% failed during final tip alignment, capping success at 50%. The Spray Graffiti task was even more unforgiving: about half the failures occurred during the initial can grasp, and 28% failed to reach the required spray area, yielding under 1% success across all baselines. On Toast Bread, every baseline failed completely (0% success). Fine-grained fingertip force modulation and precise 3D alignment remain uncharted territory for modern imitation learning.

sections.heading: The future of dexterous manipulation built on open, standardized foundations
sections.summary: DexSuite provides an open-source framework on Genesis that bridges arms, hands, and tasks for fair comparisons. It gives the research community a reproducible launchpad to tackle unsolved frontiers like sequential multi-object contact and precision tool use.
sections.details:
This work presented DexSuite, an all-in-one dexterous manipulation framework built on the Genesis simulator, accompanied by a 16-pair benchmark and 4,700 high-quality episodes. The empirical findings quantitatively show that while multi-fingered hands can match or exceed grippers on shared tasks, sequential contact transitions and fine tool manipulation pose steep hurdles for existing imitation learning methods.

DexSuite's primary strength lies in its modularity and extensibility. Researchers can add a new task simply by writing a single Python class matching the standard API. New arms, hands, and sensors can be slotted in immediately without modifying existing task logic.

By resolving the benchmark fragmentation and poor reproducibility that have long slowed dexterous robotics, DexSuite offers an open foundation where diverse research groups can benchmark algorithms on equal footing and push the field forward.

takeaways: High degrees of freedom in multi-fingered hands do not inherently hurt imitation learning; for tasks like pushing, the wider contact area of palms and fingers actually provides better stability than grippers.
Task difficulty is governed far more by discontinuous, sequential contact switches across different objects than by step horizon length alone.

Tool-use tasks requiring fine fingertip force control and precise 3D alignment, such as drill aiming or spray can actuation, yield near-zero success rates even with state-of-the-art Diffusion Policy and ACT models.

Evaluating imitation policies using peak single checkpoints leads to severe overestimation; rigorous re-evaluation across held-out seeds with at least 100 episodes is essential for credible comparisons.
limitations: Evaluations are currently confined to the Genesis simulation environment, leaving the Sim-to-Real transfer performance of the learned multi-fingered policies untested on physical robot hardware.
While tactile sensors like FlexiTac are functionally simulated, the baseline experiments do not yet evaluate policies trained with tactile readings as input observations.

On the hardest Track 2 tasks (Toast Bread and Spray Graffiti), standard imitation baselines failed almost completely (0% to 1%), offering insufficient score variance to discriminate policy quality on those challenges.
